description: Trinity is a multidisciplinary team integrating robotics, advanced AI (computer vision and predictive modeling), and software development for end-to-end telemetry and control. We look for builders in software, ML/CV, embedded hardware, UI/UX, and business strategy ready to push beyond conventional solutions. Join us to build a high-impact project!
summary:
Picture the first human on Mars, three kilometers from the habitat, facing ground no one has ever walked. Earth is 4 to 22 minutes away; there is no time to ask for instructions.

To walk safely, the first explorers need a clear view of the ground ahead, but today that information comes from rovers that are not there in real time. So we built it.

 Using open data from several NASA missions, we turned orbital images and elevation data into a multilayer map that plans safe routes around rough terrain and hazardous areas, monitors space weather, and shows how far the astronaut can go and still make it back. A scout rover goes first: if it detects a hazard invisible from orbit, it proposes a new path, the astronaut makes the final call, and Earth stays informed. We compared our routes with Perseverance's real drive through Jezero Crater, and our prototype makes it all tangible: a real rover with a live camera that follows the astronaut's voice commands and drives the planned route at scale.

This matters because the first crews will set foot where no one has been before. We help them explore farther and always make it back.
details:
"ANDAR" helps an astronaut plan and carry out a safe Marswalk, with a scout rover that walks one step ahead and a real prototype that drives the planned route.

1. Plan. The explorer picks the places to visit. "ANDAR" combines orbital images, elevation and terrain layers to draw the safest walking route: it avoids steep slopes (risky above 10°, blocked above 20°), rough ground and soft sand, explains why each route was chosen, and shows how far the astronaut can go and still walk back to the habitat.

2. Scout. During the walk, a scout rover travels one step ahead. When it reports a hazard the orbit could not see, it proposes a new path; the crew in the habitat, also on Mars, confirms it, or the astronaut can authorize it if urgent, while Earth stays informed despite the 4 to 22 minute communication delay.

3. Walk. Three views share the same mission: the habitat console, the astronaut's helmet HUD (map that follows the walker, oxygen, suit power, radiation and UV readouts, space weather) and the Earth link. A voice assistant in the HUD answers questions and turns spoken commands into rover moves.

4. Prove it. We compared our planner with Perseverance's real drive: across five sample sites (Roubion to Kukaklek) it chose the same visiting order the rover followed, with a 5.1 km walking route (Perseverance's odometer reads 11.46 km, including science stops and maneuvers). A physical prototype, a small rover with a live camera, obeys the astronaut's voice and drives the planned route at scale in a 2 × 2 m area.

Benefits

- One clear, layered view instead of data scattered across many missions and formats.

- Safety first: routes are planned within walk-back range and terrain limits, and the astronaut always sees how far is too far.

- Decisions made on Mars, by the crew, without waiting minutes for Earth.

- Explainable choices that a crew or mission planner can trust and question.

Intended impact

The first crews will walk where no one has stepped before. ANDAR turns orbital maps into decisions (where to step and when to turn back), so explorers can go farther, collect better science and always come back. The same idea serves mission planners on Earth and, today, students and the public, who can watch a real rover follow a Martian route.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

- NASA data: Mars Trek imagery of Jezero (MRO CTX and HiRISE) for the base map and sand detection; the MOLA–HRSC blended elevation model (USGS Astrogeology) for slope and terrain; Mars 2020 sampling sites and traverse (NASA/JPL) for stops and the Perseverance comparison; DONKI for space weather.

- Software: Python (FastAPI, NumPy/SciPy, Rasterio, Shapely, pymoo for the NSGA-II mission optimizer, A* for routes) and JavaScript (React, Vite, MapLibre GL, three.js), deployed on Vercel with tests, linting and security scans on every change.

- AI: Groq: Whisper turns speech into English text, and an LLM interprets commands and answers questions.

- Hardware: Raspberry Pi 4 Model B, L298N motor driver, four DC motors and a USB HD camera, streamed with µStreamer through a Cloudflare tunnel.

How it is creative

- Astronaut and rover work as a team: the robot walks first, the human decides.

- It goes beyond the screen: the same route moves a real rover, and you can talk to it.

- Our planner is compared with reality: Perseverance's own path through Jezero.

Factors we considered

- Safety: slope and terrain thresholds, a 15 km emergency walk-back limit (NASA DRA 5.0), radiation and space weather, and a STOP that overrides every other command.

- Honesty: hazards, telemetry and radiation are labeled as simulated; the rover is an Earth prototype, never presented as Mars imagery; sources are shown for every layer.

- Human factors: a quick-to-read HUD, voice control for gloved hands, and the communication delay with Earth.

- Limits and next steps: without wheel sensors the prototype drifts slightly over a route (a gyroscope or wheel encoders would fix it); next, real rover sensing instead of simulated hazards and wider HiRISE coverage beyond Jezero.
